stories.summary: In the Baroda region, Ajay saw a chemical industry complex where several private factories run pipes directly to each other. One factory's output flows through a pipe into the next factory. A meter measures how much has flowed, and the supplier invoices on that basis. No trucks, no handling, no friction.
stories.insight: This is what manufacturing looks like at its best: specialised firms sitting close together and feeding each other. Albert Hirschman called these 'linkages'. They are also why manufacturing is fragile in India. If even a few links in such a network fail, the whole ecosystem loses its advantage.
stories.quote: One of the most magical things I've seen is in the Baroda region, there's an entire chemical industry complex where there are multiple private factories who endlessly run a pipe to each other.

stories.topic: Ten Power Cuts a Day, 70 km From Bombay
stories.summary: The episode was recorded in rural Maharashtra, about 70 km from Bombay, where the power trips around ten times a day. Ajay asks how a factory could run like that. It can't, so every manufacturer buys a generator. That raises capital costs, and running a factory on diesel is ruinously expensive. Power from the grid is overpriced too, because commercial and industrial users subsidise farmers, households and electricity thieves.
stories.insight: India's electricity problem shows up close to its richest city, not just in remote corners. Each outage becomes a hidden tax on manufacturing: generators to buy, diesel to burn, and a cross-subsidy built into every grid bill.
stories.quote: we are doing this recording in rural Maharashtra, a scant 70 kilometers from Bombay. And it's astonishing how 10 times a day the MSEB power trips. Like what is this nonsense?

stories.topic: Infosys, the Import Licence and the Outdated Disk Drive
stories.summary: Amit reads an anecdote from Montek Singh Ahluwalia's memoir 'Backstage'. In 1983 Infosys wanted to import a Data General MV 8000 computer with three 200 MB disk drives. Getting the import licence took several trips to New Delhi. By the time it came through, a 300 MB drive had come out that was 30% cheaper. The licence named the exact model number, so Infosys had to make more trips to Delhi just to amend it.
stories.insight: The licence raj was not just ideologically mistaken. It could not work in practice in industries where technology changes faster than files move through ministries. For exporters racing to deliver on time, these delays were fatal.
stories.quote: By the time they got the license, a new disk drive with a capacity of 300 MB had become available. Thirty percent cheaper.

stories.topic: How India Fell From 25% to 2% of World Manufacturing
stories.summary: In 1750 India produced about 20-25% of the world's manufacturing output, all of it artisanal. By 1900 that share was about 2%. One narrative, voiced by Dadabhai Naoroji in the British Parliament, blames colonialism: cheap machine-made Manchester textiles destroyed Indian weavers. Historians such as Tirthankar Roy point to a bigger cause. The Industrial Revolution wiped out handloom workers even in countries that were never colonised. Some industrialisation did begin from the 1850s: textile mills in Bombay and Ahmedabad, jute mills in Bengal, and Tata Iron and Steel in 1907. Manufacturing's share of output roughly doubled from 3.8% in 1913 to 7.5% at Independence. Even so, only about 2.5 million of India's 350 million people worked in it.
stories.insight: The usual villain-only story misses the role of technological obsolescence. India's deeper bad luck was industrialising late. That left a thin manufacturing base for the new state to build on, and it then made things worse.
stories.quote: So it's really a shift in technology, technological obsolescence which is making this happen. And not so much just a case of colonialism. It just so happens that we got unlucky and industrialized a little later.

recommendations.item: How Frameworks (howframeworks.com)
recommendations.creator: Sudhir Sarnobat
recommendations.context: Amit's recommendation at the end of the episode. It is a new venture by Sudhir Sarnobat, a guest on Episode 419 of The Seen and the Unseen, set up with a partner whom Amit calls a legend among Maharashtra's entrepreneurs.
recommendations.reason: It offers frameworks to grow a business, turn it around or take it to the next level. Amit says these come from a lifetime of experience in Indian conditions, not consultant talk or bookish theory. Amit doesn't run a business and still spent hours going down the rabbit hole, because the frameworks also apply to how individuals live. The code 'seen unseen' gets listeners a discount; Amit takes no commission.

recommendations.reason: Friedman explains the core point clearly: a minimum wage does not raise a low-productivity worker's pay to the legal floor. It makes their job illegal, so their wage drops to zero.

core_ideas.concept: Three Numbers That Show Indian Manufacturing Is Broken
core_ideas.explanation: First, manufacturing has been stuck at 15-20% of GDP for 30 years. Countries in the middle stage of development typically reach 40-50%. Second, manufacturing's share of employment is small and not rising. Third, and most starkly, goods exports grew from $319 billion to $442 billion in a decade. That is 38% in nominal dollars, or roughly 0.5% a year in real terms. Services exports grew from $151 billion to $341 billion over the same period, a 126% rise.
core_ideas.quote: manufacturing exports growth over the last ten years of about zero point five percent per year compounded expressed in real USD, which is abysmal

core_ideas.concept: Why Services Escaped and Manufacturing Didn't
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's simple answer: IT services were new, and the state was caught off guard. No decades-old regulations were waiting for them. Manufacturing inherited a long legacy of oppressive rules. Ajay's checklist adds the structural reasons. Factories are visible, while services hide in office buildings. Manufacturing depends on dense local networks of suppliers, while services connect over fibre. Manufacturing needs land, machines and working capital, while services rent. Factories need reliable electricity. They must move physical goods, while services move electrons. They pay back over 5-7 years rather than 1-2. And they depend on a dense web of enforceable contracts.
core_ideas.quote: services, especially IT services, was relatively new for the Indian state. So it kind of got blindsided by it.

core_ideas.concept: State Legibility: Factories Are Sitting Ducks
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay borrows James C. Scott's idea of 'legibility' from Seeing Like a State. A factory is big and visible, so everyone can find it. Local goons demand protection money for trucks to pass, neighbours demand funding for pujas or schools, and every kind of inspector turns up to extort. A services firm sits on one floor of a building that looks like every other, among many firms, with no single visible owner. In a weak rule-of-law environment, being visible is a liability.
core_ideas.quote: So the first idea is that factories are sitting ducks. All the problems of extortion and expropriation by private persons and by state personnel afflict factories more.

core_ideas.explanation: Albert Hirschman argued that manufacturing's strength lies in linkages: specialised firms buying from and selling to each other nearby. Ajay imagines twenty friends planning interlinked factories within 10 km of each other near Nashik. In India, something trips up five of the ten: a labour-law problem, a bank, a local politician. The network never comes together. Services avoid this because they connect over fibre and are indifferent to location.
core_ideas.quote: So just think of it as complexity doesn't work well in India because there are too many buggy components in our Indian landscape.

core_ideas.concept: The Cathedral of Complexity Needs Contract Enforcement
core_ideas.explanation: Global manufacturing runs on just-in-time supply. If a supplier fails to deliver 5,000 ball bearings on the agreed day, the whole assembly line stops. The common-law remedy is for courts to quickly calculate liquidated damages and impose them. That lets the manufacturer recover the penalties foreign buyers impose on it. It also deters sloppiness, so suppliers move heaven and earth to deliver, even getting trucks through a political bandh. Without enforcement, firms hoard inventory or deal only with family and trusted contacts, and their competitiveness erodes.
core_ideas.quote: to do manufacturing well is to achieve a cathedral of complexity, where there's a rich array of contracts that surround the process of manufacturing and everybody works to a tight ship with lethal financial consequences when you fail.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay rejects the idea that manufacturing is a dumb, unskilled activity. A world-class export operation might hire 10,000 workers at 8,000 rupees a month. It also needs 1,000 more capable people, 100 super-capable ones and 20 global geniuses, and much of that talent doesn't exist in India yet. Sri Lanka, for example, is ahead in garment-making expertise. So India must make it effortless for companies to hire foreigners.
core_ideas.quote: To actually do manufacturing is a Herculean challenge because you're participating in global value chains with just in time delivery who are extremely demanding, who want perfect quality, perfect delivery on quantity, on date, and that's a high wire act.

core_ideas.concept: Nehru's Forgivable Mistakes, Indira's Unforgivable Ones
core_ideas.explanation: Nehru followed the fashion of the times. The Soviet Union then looked like a success, though Amit says it was mainly a public relations one. His two big mistakes were import substitution, which cut India's share of world trade from about 2% in 1947 to 0.5% by 1990, and Mahalanobis's belief that competition is wasteful. Meanwhile Hong Kong's export income in the 1960s equalled India's entire income. By 1965 the model was visibly failing, yet India went further down the same road. Amit lists the licence raj, the MRTP Act against large firms, small-scale industry reservations, FERA criminalising foreign capital, and the Industrial Disputes Act. The 1970s, when India's cheap labour could have made it a manufacturing superpower, were lost.
core_ideas.quote: What happened after 1965, frankly, is unforgivable. We knew we were on the wrong track and we deepened our journey into that wrong track.

core_ideas.concept: Why India's MSMEs Are Mostly Micro
core_ideas.explanation: Under the Industrial Disputes Act, a firm with 100 or more workers needed government permission to fire anyone, and in practice permission was impossible to get. Other rules kicked in at 10 and 20 workers. Firms responded by staying at 9, 19 or 99 employees and splitting into separate units to grow. The threshold was recently raised to 300, which Amit still calls absurd. The 'small' and 'medium' in MSME barely exist. Laws meant to protect workers end up hurting them. Amit adds that big companies aren't bad: large profits mean a firm serves many people well at scale.
core_ideas.quote: It's a classic example of why you should judge a policy not by its intention, but by its outcome.

core_ideas.concept: Minimum Wages and Unions Hurt the Poor
core_ideas.explanation: Take a worker whose labour is worth 8,000 rupees. A 13,000-rupee minimum wage doesn't raise his pay. It makes his job illegal, so he earns zero. The job he took was his best available option, and in a competitive market a rival employer would pay more if his work were worth more. Ajay describes it as the state using its monopoly of violence to block a voluntary deal between consenting adults. One result is capital-intensive garment factories in a country with mass unemployment. Ajay also notes that unions are a form of market power, a market failure the state should counteract rather than entrench.
core_ideas.quote: So what you really do is with a minimum wage you put the poorest people out of a job, which is just criminal

core_ideas.explanation: A village of 150 households has about 750 people, perhaps 300 of working age, and at most about 100 would go to one factory. A globally competitive plant needs well over 2,000 workers. A factory with 10,000 machines also needs maintenance vendors and managers, and those people need offices, homes and schools for their children. So factories belong near cities, built into planning with higher FSI for multi-storey plants and matching road and rail links. Ajay finds the Chinese dormitory model deeply dissatisfying. He also notes that land prices look like a China-style bubble.
core_ideas.quote: So you should get out of the romantic idea that there will be factories near villages.

core_ideas.explanation: Commercial and industrial users are overcharged for grid power to subsidise agriculture, free household units and outright theft. Supply is also unreliable. Then Europe, the UK and others are introducing carbon border taxes. An Indian exporter pays for some of the world's most expensive and intermittent electricity, and then pays again at the border because that power is carbon-intensive. Exporters also cannot buy certifiable, auditable 100% renewable power. Ajay says Gujarat works reasonably well, and other states do badly.
core_ideas.quote: There cannot be a factory without excellent electricity. And India is a fail.

core_ideas.explanation: Any friction at the border makes imported inputs dearer and Indian manufacturers less competitive. Ajay's example: the yarn that goes into artificial (non-cotton) fabric is the world's most important, and India puts a 10% duty on it. That makes all synthetic fabric in India 10% dearer than in Bangladesh or Vietnam, which hurts the entire garment industry.
core_ideas.quote: If you want to be globally competitive, you need raw materials at global prices.

core_ideas.concept: The Bankruptcy Code as the Fix for Late Payments
core_ideas.explanation: Big Indian companies routinely squeeze small suppliers on payments. Ajay calls this short-sighted, since big firms have access to cheaper capital and would get better procurement by paying promptly. The fix is not a government invoice portal. It is strict enforcement of whatever payment terms were freely agreed, through a bankruptcy code that empowers operational creditors. The current code was shaped by big companies, which won protections against such creditors. Push ten important big companies into bankruptcy over unpaid suppliers, Ajay says, and everyone else will get the message.
core_ideas.quote: I should not have to do chakar to your office and pay you Diwali gifts in the hope of getting paid.

core_ideas.explanation: Shubho Roy, a law academic at Shiv Nadar University and a friend of the hosts, has long campaigned on this. If you owe 100 rupees, stall for 10 years in court, and are then ordered to pay 100 rupees at 5% interest, you have got a cheap loan. Courts should apply punitive interest rates so that defaulting on a contract costs more than honouring it.
core_ideas.quote: Okay, so the interest rates used by courts in their calculations need to be punitive, so that you will think five times before you renege on a payment.

core_ideas.explanation: When goods are exported, every bit of indirect tax paid along the way should be refunded. Elsewhere in the world, VAT is fully refunded at the point of export. India's GST and RoDTEP refund only part of it. Several taxes are never refunded, and delays in refunds tie up working capital. Indian exporters therefore carry tax that their competitors don't.
core_ideas.quote: The fundamental principle of taxation is you do not tax non residents.

core_ideas.explanation: Wright's Law: each doubling of a firm's cumulative lifetime output brings about a 20% gain in productivity. In a factory with 10,000 machines, even a 0.1% efficiency gain per machine adds up to serious money, so complex optimisations pay off. Small factories can't justify them. India celebrates 2,000-worker factories, but successful low-cost manufacturers run 10,000 to 100,000 workers, and India's system trips up anything that grows big.
core_ideas.quote: In a very big factory, if you have ten thousand machines, every subtle optimization is worth it.

core_ideas.concept: The Indian State as an Autarky
core_ideas.explanation: Global manufacturing means constant travel, cross-border contracts, foreign bank accounts and arbitration abroad. The Indian state distrusts all of it. A tax officer who finds a foreign bank account suspects hawala. Ajay suggests a simple fix: the UK lets people hold two passports, so one can be away getting a visa while you travel on the other. India makes this hard, which slows down how often executives can travel.
core_ideas.quote: The entire Indian state is organized as an autarky.

core_ideas.concept: Twelve Problems: Five for the Union, Seven for the States
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's checklist of what holds manufacturing back: labour law and minimum wages; infrastructure (no longer the binding constraint); land; locating the workforce; electricity; trade barriers; finance; an anti-globalisation state; hostility to size; dispute resolution; tax refunds on exports; and the skilled-labour gap. Five of the twelve are in the union government's hands and seven are with the states. That explains why Gujarat, Maharashtra, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu have pulled ahead. Every state should run its own growth strategy on its seven.
core_ideas.quote: But actually each state is a master of its own destiny on seven out of the twelve things.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit on Ajay praising his MSME episode: it's like a novice songwriter taking his song to Bob Dylan and Dylan saying 'Wow, this is such a great song.' For Amit to do a manufacturing episode and have Ajay call it good 'is exactly the same thing.'

Ajay says everyone should put the checklist of manufacturing problems up in their bathroom and 'worship every day'. Amit replies: 'You are the kind of economist who actually has lists in his bathroom about how to make Indian manufacturing better… Actually I don't have any lists, so there's nothing embarrassing there. There are shower gels and shampoos, but let's not go there again.'

Before recording, while going through pointers on industrial policy and labour laws, Ajay declared he was having so much fun. Amit: 'Bhai, you are having fun. I'm trying to memorize phrases, you are having fun.'
Ajay boasts that services exports grew 126% in a decade, 'nothing to sneeze at'. Amit: 'That happened to my weight, but continue.'

Ajay adapts Shakespeare's Julius Caesar to describe Indian supply chains: 'Then burst his mighty heart, and muffling up his face, even at the base of Pompey's statue, great Caesar fell… Ingratitude more strong than traitors' arms vanquished him. No, I want to say incompetence more strong than traitors' arms vanquished him.'

Ajay's 'North Korea-South Korea comparison': 'a communist country called West Bengal, where the minimum wage is 13,000 rupees, and a capitalist country called East Bengal' with a minimum wage of 7,000-8,000. Guess which one built the successful garment export industry.
Ajay grants that Maharashtra has reined in wildcat unions, then adds: 'I will point out that there are many states in India that are not called Maharashtra.'
Ajay says a 2,000-worker factory 'ain't much' globally. Amit jokes: 'Some would dream of a factory with 1.7 billion people… Manufacturing national pride.'
Amit on the Nehru era: the world didn't yet know the Soviet Union was 'a complete and utter failure. It was really a public relations success.'
Amit after Ajay's twelve-point diagnosis: 'I will watch this episode again and again and again and maybe get our editor to do a version of it that doesn't have me and only you.'
Charlie Chaplin's 'Modern Times' is Ajay's shorthand for the romantic dream of manufacturing: tens of thousands of obedient workers on an assembly line.
James C. Scott's idea of 'legibility' from Seeing Like a State, used to explain why visible factories attract extortion from goons and inspectors.
Albert Hirschman's 'linkages': the network effects created when specialised factories buy from and sell to each other.
Adam Smith's pin factory, cited for the principle that each factory should do one thing well instead of one campus doing twenty things badly.
Frédéric Bastiat's 'the seen and the unseen', the phrase Amit named his podcast after. He invokes it for the vast unseen costs of FERA-style capital controls.
Dadabhai Naoroji's criticism in the British Parliament that cheap Manchester textiles destroyed India's artisanal weavers.

P.C. Mahalanobis's mid-1950s claim that competition is wasteful ('Why should two companies make cars, one is enough'). Amit notes it still underlies laws today: 'Why should ten people make potato chips?'
